channel.title: Lab Members on Bionic Vision Lab
channel.description: Recent content in Lab Members on Bionic Vision Lab

item.description:
Sahiti Doke is an undergraduate student pursuing a Mathematics degree in the College of Creative Studies at UC Santa Barbara. She is currently working on improving neural models using mechanistic interpretability techniques. She is also interested in mathematics, more specifically abstract algebra.

In her free time, she enjoys listening to J-pop, playing rhythm games, and cursing Netflix executives for axing Inside Job after a single season.

Christian Grunt is an undergraduate student studying Computer Engineering at UC Santa Barbara, with experience in machine learning and embedded systems. He is particularly interested in the intersection of neuroscience and computing, and how these fields can advance the development of artificial intelligence. In the Bionic Vision Lab, Christian applies his software development skills, especially in building virtual environments using the Unity Engine, to support research on human vision.

Outside of the lab, he enjoys competing in volleyball, playing board games, and creating digital illustrations.

Yuchen Hou is a PhD candidate in Computer Science at UC Santa Barbara. She studies active vision: how intelligent systems combine visual input with movement, behavior, and internal state to make sense of the world.

Her research sits at the intersection of computational neuroscience and machine learning. She develops multimodal and recurrent models of neural activity during natural behavior, with work spanning visual cortex, eye and head movements, and the dynamics of active visual sampling. Her broader goal is to uncover computational principles of biological vision that can inform more robust and behaviorally grounded AI systems.

Yuchen earned her B.S. in Psychological & Brain Sciences from UC Santa Barbara before continuing into the Computer Science PhD program. She completed a research internship at Google in 2026, and her earlier work was recognized with UCSB’s Exceptional Academic Performance Award and the Abdullah & Marjorie R. Nasser Memorial Scholarship.

Outside of the lab, Yuchen enjoys reading fiction and watching action movies.

Karolina Huang is an undergraduate at UC Santa Barbara pursuing a dual degree in Psychological & Brain Sciences (BS) and Statistics & Data Science (BA). She is interested in computational modeling of vision science to understand how visual information is processed at the neuronal level and to advance knowledge about the brain mechanisms of different visual impairments.

Outside of research, Karolina enjoys making dessert and playing volleyball.

Emily Joyce is a PhD student in Dynamical Neuroscience at UC Santa Barbara. She studies how the retina encodes visual information and how that neural code might be recreated through artificial stimulation.

Her research uses cell- and circuit-level computational modeling to understand how retinal prostheses interact with the neural circuitry that remains after vision loss. Her dissertation focuses on next-generation implants that directly stimulate retinal bipolar cells, asking how patterns of stimulation could produce richer and more natural visual percepts, including color. Her long-term goal is to use biologically grounded models of the retina to guide the design and programming of future visual prostheses.

Before joining the Bionic Vision Lab, Emily worked with large-scale electron microscopy connectomics datasets at Janelia and the Allen Institute, studying cell types and neural circuitry in sensory systems and developing open-source tools for analyzing neuronal morphology and connectivity. She is a UCSB Regents Fellow and an inaugural UC Noyce Graduate Student Fellow, one of five doctoral students selected across the University of California.

Outside of the lab, Emily enjoys gardening, training her dogs, and learning to surf.

Ryan is an undergraduate student at UC Santa Barbara pursuing a BS in Physics. He is interested in vision science and sensory processing, and in particular research that combines experimental work with computational theory and modeling to understand how visual information is represented in real-world applications.

Outside of research, Ryan enjoys playing piano, teaching music to youth, and practicing Muay Thai.

Will is an undergraduate student majoring in Biopsychology and minoring in chemistry. He has always been interested in how neuroscience can explain human behavior. This led him to get involved with the Szumlinski lab, where he continues to learn more about the biochemical mechanisms of addiction.

He currently serves as the lead research assistant for psychophysical data collection in a collaborative project between the Bionic Vision Lab and the Louis Lab, helping coordinate behavioral experiments and data collection.

Outside of research, Will likes to play tennis and this video game called Overwatch. He also enjoys helping other students with chemistry and volunteering with local elementary schools to educate kids about the brain.

Diego Linn is an undergraduate student pursuing a Computer Science degree at UC Santa Barbara. Diego is interested in how innovations in machine learning can be applied to understanding our vision. He is fascinated by the possible applications of immersive technology and its ability to create positive change. In the Bionic Vision Lab, his goal is to explore how immersive technology, machine learning, and computer science can be combined to improve lives and the understanding of our neural pathways.

In his free time, Diego loves to read fantasy and sci-fi books, write some of his own, and explore Santa Barbara’s gorgeous coastline.

Jack Liu is currently an undergraduate Computer Science student at the University of California, Santa Barbara. He is interested in artificial intelligence, computer vision, and building projects that solve real-world problems. He is particularly drawn to developing things that connect technology and human impact. Through the Bionic Vision Lab, he hopes to continue exploring computer vision and contribute to work that benefits those in need.

In his free time, Jack loves to go thrifting, watch movies, and read manga.
Samantha Lund is working toward a BS in Biopsychology at UC Santa Barbara.

Lucas Nadolskis is a PhD student in Dynamical Neuroscience at UC Santa Barbara. He studies how visual experience shapes the brain, asking just how nonvisual the “visual” brain can become when vision is absent.

His research lies at the intersection of computational neuroscience and NeuroAI, using machine learning and representational analysis to compare how biological and artificial systems encode information. His work has examined the relationship between deep neural network representations and activity in blind visual cortex, and his dissertation aims to use NeuroAI models to understand how sensory experience, plasticity, and task demands shape the organization of the human brain.

Lucas also has extensive experience in accessibility research and leadership, including work on assistive AI, accessible data visualization, and visual neuroprostheses. He is a recipient of the UCSB Regents Fellowship and has served in advisory and organizing roles across the accessibility research community. He earned his B.S. in Computer Science from the University of Minnesota and his M.S. in Computational Biomedical Engineering from Carnegie Mellon University.

Outside of the lab, Lucas enjoys music, traveling, and searching for good audio-described content.

William is an undergraduate student majoring in Computer Science. His interests include game design, extended reality, and artificial intelligence, with a particular interest in connecting these areas through research and creative work. He is involved in research with the Four Eyes Lab, where he contributes XR expertise, supports cross-lab collaboration, and explores topics in machine learning, multimodal models, and 3D scene analysis.

In the Bionic Vision Lab, he serves as the lead Unity developer for a collaborative project with the Louis Lab, helping develop the experimental framework for immersive behavioral studies.

Galen Pogoncheff is a PhD candidate in Computer Science at UC Santa Barbara. He studies how the internal representations of biological and artificial neural networks give rise to behavior.

His research spans NeuroAI, representation learning, and AI alignment. He has developed biologically constrained neural networks to identify computational principles that make artificial models more brain-like, and his current work asks how the structure of learned representations can be used to transfer desirable behaviors such as robustness between models. His broader goal is to uncover general principles linking representation, computation, and behavior in intelligent systems.

Galen earned his B.S. and M.S. in Computer Science from the University of Colorado Boulder. He has completed multiple research internships at Meta, including work on machine learning for neural interfaces, and is a recipient of the UCSB CCS Community Fellowship and the Computer Science Outstanding TA Award.

Outside of the lab, Galen enjoys spending time in the mountains and at the gym.

Marius Schneider is a Postdoctoral Scholar in the Bionic Vision Lab at UC Santa Barbara. He studies how brains and artificial systems transform sensory input into action through closed sensorimotor loops.

His research combines systems neuroscience, computational modeling, and NeuroAI to understand perception during natural behavior. He has used large-scale spike and field-potential recordings to study neural dynamics in freely moving animals, and now develops digital twins and biologically inspired models that link visual input, internal state, movement, and behavior. His current work extends these ideas toward human navigation and neuromorphic systems that can make fast, low-power decisions in the real world.

Marius completed his doctoral research at the Ernst Strüngmann Institute and earned his PhD in Neurophysics from Radboud University with highest honors. He is a recipient of the EBBS Young Investigator Award and the 2026–27 James V. & Beverly R. Zaleski Discovery Award in Robotics and Computing.

Outside of the lab, Marius enjoys running, working out, spending time at the beach, traveling, and listening to music.

Eirini Schoinas is an undergraduate researcher in Computing at UC Santa Barbara’s College of Creative Studies. She develops computational methods for neural interfaces, with a particular interest in the software and algorithms that translate neural stimulation into useful function.

Her research combines computational neuroscience, machine learning, and neuroengineering. In the Bionic Vision Lab, she has developed models of how electrical stimulation produces neural activity and visual percepts, with recent work focused on predicting phosphene patterns produced by stimulation of the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN). More broadly, she is interested in algorithmic approaches to brain-computer interfaces and other neurotechnologies that connect artificial systems with the nervous system.

Eirini is a 2026 Barry Goldwater Scholar and received an Honorable Mention for the Computing Research Association’s Outstanding Undergraduate Researcher Award, as well as a UCSB College of Creative Studies Summer Undergraduate Research Fellowship. She has presented her research at the IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Conference.

Outside of the lab, Eirini enjoys reading, hiking, and making art.

Hannah is an undergraduate student at UC Santa Barbara pursuing a double major in Biopsychology and Dance on the pre-optometry track. She is passionate about bringing together the arts and sciences to develop a well-rounded perspective and expand her understanding of perception and behavior.

In the Bionic Vision Lab, she advanced from Junior Lab Trainee to Senior Research Assistant in Spring ‘26, where she is contributing to psychophysical data collection in a collaborative project between the Bionic Vision Lab and the Louis Lab.

Hannah Stone is a PhD student in Psychological & Brain Sciences at UC Santa Barbara. She studies how the brain turns artificial stimulation into conscious visual experience.

Her research combines psychophysics, neurostimulation, EEG analysis, and computational modeling to understand how cortical activity gives rise to visual percepts. Her current work uses TMS to study phosphene perception and is building toward combining stimulation with EEG to examine how brain state influences whether and what a person sees. In parallel, she develops computational models of V1 to better predict the perceptual consequences of cortical stimulation. In 2026, she received the Richard E. Mayer Award for the best second-year paper in the department.

Before joining the Bionic Vision Lab, Hannah worked at Stanford University, where she studied how task demands and individual differences shape the neural processing of written language. She previously conducted research at the University of Rochester on how attention influences eye movements and early visual processing.

Outside of the lab, Hannah enjoys painting, surfing, and exploring Santa Barbara by bike.

Nora Thomas is an undergraduate honors student in Biopsychology at UC Santa Barbara. She studies how the brain represents the visual world, with a particular interest in mid-level visual properties such as color and texture.

Her research interests lie at the intersection of visual neuroscience and computational neuroscience. She is interested in combining human neuroimaging with computational models to understand how visual representations emerge and transform across the visual system, and in using insights from NeuroAI to compare biological and artificial vision. More broadly, she hopes to understand how neural computations give rise to the rich perceptual structure of everyday vision.

Nora joined the Bionic Vision Lab as a research assistant in Summer 2025 and became the lab manager in Fall 2026 while continuing her honors research.

Outside of the lab, Nora enjoys dancing, reading, and sewing.

Lily Turkstra is a PhD candidate in Psychological & Brain Sciences at UC Santa Barbara. She studies the human side of sight restoration, asking what happens after vision is restored and how people learn to make useful sense of artificial vision.

Her research examines how people who are blind use assistive technologies, how visual prosthesis users experience artificial vision in daily life, and how attention, engagement, and cognitive state shape performance. Her dissertation focuses on visual rehabilitation, including gamified training and neurofeedback, with the long-term goal of developing personalized approaches that help people make better use of restored vision.

Lily earned her B.S. in Psychology, with minors in Biology and Music, from Cal Poly San Luis Obispo, where she conducted psychoacoustic research in the Multisensory Perception Lab. Before beginning her PhD, she served as lab manager of the Bionic Vision Lab.

Outside of the lab, Lily enjoys tidepooling, playing bass, and biking around Santa Barbara.

Apurv Varshney is a PhD student in Computer Science at UC Santa Barbara. He develops computer vision and interactive systems that help people navigate complex environments more effectively.

His research sits at the intersection of computer vision, human-computer interaction, and extended reality. His dissertation focuses on the “last mile” of navigation for people who are blind or have low vision, including how wearable cameras can capture useful spatial information and how that information should be translated into intuitive guidance. More broadly, he studies how sensing, scene understanding, and interface design can work together to support real-time movement and decision-making.

Apurv earned his B.Tech. in Computer Science from the Indian Institute of Technology Goa. He leads development of the lab’s BionicVisionXR platform for building and evaluating immersive visual-assistance systems, and received the UCSB Computer Science Outstanding TA Award in 2025.

Outside of the lab, Apurv enjoys biking and playing tennis.
